Firstborn
FIRST-born
n.
First + born; renders the Hebrew b’khor (firstborn) and the Greek prōtotokos (firstborn). In Scripture often a title of preeminence and inheritance as well as of literal birth-order.

See also: Firstborn

📖 Biblical Definition

The firstborn in Scripture is a title of both inheritance-priority and preeminence, applied first to literal firstborn sons (Esau, Reuben, etc.), then to Israel as God’s firstborn among the nations (Israel is my son, even my firstborn, Ex 4:22), and supremely to Christ across the New Testament epistles, where the title carries the highest Christological weight. The Hebrew b’khor belonged to the firstborn son with significant rights: a double portion of the inheritance (Deut 21:17), the headship of the family, and (where applicable) the priestly and kingly succession. The narrative tension across Genesis is the unexpected displacement of natural firstborns—Cain by Abel/Seth, Ishmael by Isaac, Esau by Jacob, Reuben by Judah/Joseph, Manasseh by Ephraim—each pointing forward to the supreme Firstborn who would not be displaced. Christ is named firstborn in several New Testament texts with deep Christological substance. Colossians 1:15: who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature. The verse has been historically used by Arians to make Christ a creature; the orthodox reading (vindicated by the immediate context, vv. 16-17, which identify Him as the One by whom were all things created and before all things) takes firstborn here in the sense of preeminence-and-inheritance over creation, not as a member of it. Romans 8:29 names Him the firstborn among many brethren, those whom the Father predestined to be conformed to His image; Colossians 1:18 names Him the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence; Revelation 1:5 names Him the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth; Hebrews 1:6 speaks of when he bringeth in the firstbegotten into the world and commands the angels to worship Him. The Firstborn category is therefore Christological at its highest reach: Christ is Firstborn over all creation (Col 1:15), Firstborn from the dead (Col 1:18; Rev 1:5), Firstborn among many brethren (Rom 8:29). The redeemed are the church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven (Heb 12:23)—sharing, by union with Christ, in His firstborn-inheritance. The doctrine therefore holds Christ’s supremacy at its center and the redeemed’s participation by union as its consequence: He is Firstborn over all things and the saints are partakers of His inheritance, His resurrection, His glory, in the proportion determined by their union with Him.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FIRSTBORN as first brought forth; eldest; in scripture, a title of inheritance-priority and preeminence applied to Israel as God’s firstborn among the nations and supremely to Christ as Firstborn of creation, from the dead, and among many brethren.

FIRSTBORN, a. or n. — First brought forth; first born; eldest. The firstborn of every creature (Col 1:15). In scripture, a title of inheritance-priority and of preeminence applied to literal firstborn sons, to Israel, and supremely to Christ.

BIRTHRIGHT, n. — The right, privileges, or possession to which a person is entitled by birth; especially, the rights of the firstborn son under the law of Moses.

📖 Key Scripture

Colossians 1:15 — "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature."

Colossians 1:18 — "And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence."

Romans 8:29 — "For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren."

Hebrews 12:23 — "To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The firstborn doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the Arian heresy that has historically read Col 1:15 as making Christ a created firstborn rather than the preeminent Firstborn over creation—and on the other by the loss of the inheritance-and-preeminence sense in modern reading that flattens the title to mere birth-order without its weighty covenantal and Christological substance.

expand to see more

The Arian reading of Colossians 1:15 is the historic corruption of the firstborn doctrine and a corruption the orthodox church has consistently identified and refuted. The firstborn of every creature, read as a member of creation born first, makes Christ a creature and denies the deity Colossians and the whole New Testament uniformly affirm. The immediate context refutes the reading: verses 16-17 identify Christ as by whom were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, and as the One who is before all things, and by him all things consist. A created Christ cannot create all things and be before all things; the reading must therefore be the orthodox one: firstborn here carries the Hebrew sense of preeminence-and-inheritance (cf. Ps 89:27, I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth—David, who was the youngest of his brothers, is called firstborn by appointment of preeminence). Christ is the Firstborn over creation in this sense: preeminent, inheritor of all things, the One in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwells.

The opposite corruption is the modern reading that flattens the title to mere birth-order without its weighty covenantal and Christological substance. The firstborn in the Bible is not chiefly a chronological designation but a covenantal one: the firstborn son inherits, leads, exercises priestly and kingly functions, represents the family. When Scripture names Christ the firstborn from the dead, it names not merely the first chronologically to rise (Lazarus and others were raised before Him, though not to glorified life) but the One whose resurrection is the firstfruits and pattern of all subsequent resurrections, the One who inherits the resurrection-glory He shares with His brethren, the One whose preeminence in resurrection is the ground of His preeminence in everything. Recover the inheritance-and-preeminence sense, and the Firstborn doctrine recovers its full Christological weight: Christ Firstborn over creation, Firstborn from the dead, Firstborn among many brethren—the supreme Firstborn whose inheritance the redeemed share by union with Him.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew b’khor (firstborn) and Greek prōtotokos (firstborn)—a title of inheritance-priority and preeminence applied to Israel as God’s firstborn among the nations and supremely to Christ as Firstborn over creation (Col 1:15), Firstborn from the dead (Col 1:18; Rev 1:5), and Firstborn among many brethren (Rom 8:29).

expand to see more

Hebrew b’khor (H1060) — firstborn (Ex 4:22, Israel as God’s firstborn; Deut 21:17, the firstborn’s double portion).

Greek prōtotokos (G4416) — firstborn (Col 1:15, 18; Rom 8:29; Heb 1:6; 12:23; Rev 1:5).

Hebrew b’khorāh (H1062) — birthright (Gen 25:31-34, sold by Esau for a bowl of pottage).

Greek prōtotōkia (G4415) — birthright (Heb 12:16, Esau’s birthright).

Usage

"Firstborn of every creature (Col 1:15) carries the Hebrew sense of preeminence-and-inheritance, not creaturehood—Christ is over creation, not in it as a member."

"Christ is Firstborn over creation, Firstborn from the dead, and Firstborn among many brethren—a threefold title spanning creation, resurrection, and the redeemed."

"The Arian reading flattens Col 1:15 into creaturehood; the modern reading flattens firstborn into mere birth-order; the orthodox reading holds the covenantal-Christological substance."
